teaser: Cast in one pour of molten metal, about six hundred years ago, with no second chance.
review_notes:
The catalog year 1350 is approximate; the British Museum dates the head to the 14th or early 15th century.
Metal: the head is a leaded brass (copper alloy with zinc and lead), commonly called bronze.
Height about 35 cm.
Found in January 1938 at Wunmonije Compound, Ife, with other heads (usually counted as seventeen in total); acquired by the British Museum in 1939.
Frobenius's 1910 Atlantis theory.
Purpose of the holes around the mouth and meaning of the facial lines are uncertain; presented as hypotheses.
Identification as an Ooni (king) rests on the crown.
Use of an Ife head as emblem of the 1973 All-Africa Games in Lagos.
The photo is taken from the front in low light; the neck is in shadow and not pointed at.

lesson.text: Everything about this face was decided in a few seconds. Somewhere in the city of Ife, in what is now southwestern Nigeria, a caster tipped a crucible of glowing liquid metal into a clay mold. The metal ran into a gap only a few millimeters wide, filled it, and cooled. What you see is that instant, hardened.

The method is called lost-wax casting. The sculptor models the head in wax over a clay core, with every line and bead in place. The wax is wrapped in more clay and heated. It melts and runs out, leaving a hollow in its exact shape. Metal goes in where the wax was. The mold is then broken, so each head can be made only once.
Lost-wax casting gives one attempt. A cold spot, a trapped bubble or a cracked mold ruins months of work, and a casting this thin-walled and complete is a feat by any standard.

The head stands about 35 centimeters high (14 inches), a little under life size. People call it bronze, but tests show mostly copper and zinc with some lead, which makes it brass. It was made around the 14th or early 15th century. And the wax model that the metal replaced was something special.

lesson.title: What the wax recorded
lesson.text: The caster kept every decision the modeler made. Three of them are worth a slow look.

spots.title: A real face
spots.text: The eyelids have thickness. The cheeks swell gently and the nostrils flare. The proportions are those of a living person, calm and idealized, with no exaggeration.

spots.title: The lines
spots.text: Fine parallel grooves run down the whole face, bending with each curve of the forehead. They may show scar patterns worn on the skin, or stand for the shadow of a veil. Nobody knows for sure.

spots.title: The mouth
spots.text: Full lips, closed and level, with clean edges. There is no smile and no frown. The expression is composure, the look of someone who is watched and does not react.

lesson.text: That composure fits the hat. Ife was a rich city-state of the Yoruba people and, in Yoruba belief, the place where the world began. Its ruler bears the title Ooni. The tiered headdress with its crest is a crown, so this is very likely a king, or the idea of one.

The head came to light in January 1938, when workers digging foundations for a house in Ife struck metal. Seventeen heads came out of the ground at that spot, a short walk from the royal palace. This one reached London the next year, and nearly all the others stayed in Nigeria.

Europe did not know what to do with them. In 1910 the German explorer Leo Frobenius had seen similar pieces in Ife and announced that he had found the lost Greek colony of Atlantis. He could not imagine such naturalism, such a lifelike treatment of the body, coming from African hands. The 1938 find made that position impossible to hold.
The Ife heads forced art historians to redraw their map. Lifelike portraiture and expert metal casting had grown up in West Africa independently, generations before Europeans sailed down that coast.

The photograph here is taken from straight ahead, in dim museum light, and that suits the object. Some marks on it are still unexplained. As you move around, think about what might once have been attached, and what the head was for.

spots.title: Holes around the lips
spots.text: A row of small holes circles the mouth and jaw. Something was fixed there: perhaps a beaded veil hiding the king's mouth, perhaps a beard of hair. The holes were made on purpose in the wax.

spots.title: The rosette
spots.text: A disc of raised rings with a pointed center sits on the front of the crown, like a badge of office.

spots.title: The crest
spots.text: A braided stem rises from the rosette and ends in a pointed bud. It leans slightly, bent at some moment in six centuries.

spots.title: Rows of beads
spots.text: The crown is built in tiers of tube-shaped beads, each modeled separately. Ife was a center of glass bead making, and beads meant royalty.

spots.title: Traces of red
spots.text: The rusty color on the band is old paint. The crown was once colored, probably to imitate red stone and blue glass beads.

spots.title: An eye
spots.text: The upper lid overlaps the lower at the outer corner, an observed detail. There is no pupil. The gaze is blank and steady.

lesson.text: Nigerians know this face well. An Ife head served as the emblem of the All-Africa Games held in Lagos in 1973, and the image has appeared on logos and souvenirs ever since.

Nobody wrote down what the heads were used for. One idea is that each was fixed to a wooden body and dressed in real robes for a ceremony after a ruler's death, standing in for him one last time. If that is right, this face was never meant to be seen bare, in a glass case, by strangers. Does knowing that change how you meet its eyes?

quiz.question: Why can a lost-wax casting be made only once?
options: The metal is too expensive to reuse
The wax model melts away and the mold is broken
The law of Ife forbade copies
quiz.explanation: The wax is lost in heating and the clay mold is destroyed to free the metal.

quiz.question: What is the head actually made of?
options: Brass, mostly copper and zinc with some lead
quiz.explanation: It is called bronze by habit, but tests show a leaded brass.

quiz.question: How was the head discovered?
options: It was always kept in the palace
A diver found it in a river
Workers digging house foundations in 1938 struck it
quiz.explanation: Seventeen heads were found at the same building site in Ife.

quiz.question: What did Leo Frobenius claim in 1910?
options: That the Ife works were modern fakes
That they came from a lost Greek colony, Atlantis
That they were made in Egypt
quiz.explanation: He could not accept that such lifelike art was African.

quiz.question: What might the holes around the mouth have held?
options: A beaded veil or a beard
quiz.explanation: Something was attached there, though no one is certain what.

facts.text: The sculptor could recast the head from the same mold if the pour failed.
facts.explanation: The mold is broken to release the casting, so there is only one attempt.

facts.text: The headdress identifies the figure as a probable king of Ife.
facts.explanation: The tiered, crested headdress is a crown, linked to the ruler called the Ooni.

facts.text: The lines on the face are cracks caused by age.
facts.explanation: They are grooves modeled on purpose, perhaps scar patterns or the sign of a veil.
